case_name: United States v. American Institute of Certified Public Accountants and National Association of State Boards of Accountancy
court: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts (administrative settlement)
docket: Administrative — no federal court docket; U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Massachusetts
industry_specific: Professional accounting certification body and licensing administrator
defendant_name: American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) and National Association of State Boards of Accountancy (NASBA)
claim_type: ADA Title III — Uniform CPA Exam computer-based testing system inaccessible to blind and low-vision test-takers; screen reader and magnification software incompatible with exam platform and Authoritative Literature database
settlement_disclosed: $15,000 to named complainant Jane Doe; $1,000–$10,000 to additional aggrieved persons identified by the DOJ
estimated_costs: $15,000+ direct payments + technology remediation (JAWS screen reader + ZoomText Magnifier/Reader integration for full exam)

sources.name: DOJ — Settlement Agreement between the United States and AICPA and NASBA (archive.ada.gov)
DOJ USAO Massachusetts — U.S. Attorney's Office Settles Disability Discrimination Allegations Related to the CPA Exam

violation_source_evidence: DOJ Settlement Agreement (archive.ada.gov/cpa_exam_sa.html): 'there was no screen reader software for certain portions of the Exam, including the Authoritative Literature.' JAWS Screen Reader and ZoomText Magnifier/Reader were unavailable for portions of the computer-based CPA exam. Test-takers received 'a software-related auxiliary aid that was not appropriate or a reader that was not qualified or appropriate.' JAWS made available as of November 2017 for the Authoritative Literature; ZoomText for entirety of exam.
summary_one_line: DOJ forced the AICPA and NASBA — the accounting profession's own gatekeepers — to make the Uniform CPA Exam accessible to blind candidates, paying $15,000+ in damages and integrating JAWS and ZoomText across the entire exam platform.
notes: Complaint filed by Jane Doe, a low-vision/legally blind CPA candidate who requested screen magnification and reader software but was offered only a human reader instead. DOJ investigation launched August 2017. Settlement effective April 1, 2019. By November 2017 (before settlement), AICPA had already deployed ZoomText Magnifier/Reader for all exam sections and made Authoritative Literature accessible via JAWS Screen Reader. This is an exceptionally ironic B2B case: the AICPA is the body that sets professional standards for the entire accounting industry. Ongoing commitments include biannual reporting for 2 years and evaluation of emerging accessibility technologies. The 'irony angle': professional gatekeepers for accountants had inaccessible digital testing infrastructure.
